posts.title: Extended thinking + tools is the real unlock
posts.hook: Claude's extended thinking combined with tool use doesn't get enough attention. It's not a feature. It's a different kind of agent.
posts.body:
Claude's extended thinking combined with tool use doesn't get enough attention. It's not a feature. It's a different kind of agent.

I've been running Claude Code with extended thinking on multi-step GTM builds for months now. The difference between a model that reasons through a problem before touching a tool vs. one that just fires API calls sequentially is night and day.

Example from this week: I asked it to build an enrichment pipeline that pulls from three data providers, deduplicates on domain, scores by ICP fit, and pushes to Attio. Without extended thinking, it builds each step in isolation and you get a Frankenstein pipeline. With it, the agent maps the full data flow first, catches edge cases in the schema before writing a line of code, and produces something that actually runs clean on the first pass.

The practical difference: I stopped debugging agent output. I went from reviewing every intermediate step to reviewing the final result.

Most people are benchmarking this on coding puzzles and math problems. The real benchmark is whether your agent can hold a 15-step workflow in its head and make coherent decisions across all of them. That's where extended thinking changes the economics of building with agents.
posts.cta: If you're building with Claude Code and haven't turned on extended thinking for complex workflows, try it on your next multi-step build. The difference compounds.

remixes.label: before-after-breakdown
remixes.hook: I ran the same GTM build twice. Once with extended thinking off, once with it on. The second run caught three errors the first one introduced.
remixes.body:
I ran the same GTM build twice. Once with extended thinking off, once with it on. The second run caught three errors the first one introduced.

Without extended thinking, Claude Code operates like a fast junior dev. It grabs the first tool that seems right, fires the call, gets a result, moves on. When something breaks downstream, it patches. When the patch breaks something else, it patches again. You end up with a working pipeline held together with duct tape.

With extended thinking, the behavior shifts. The model pauses before each tool call. It considers what data it actually needs, which API endpoint returns it in the right shape, and whether the downstream step can consume the output format. It plans the sequence before executing it.

This week I watched it reason through a three-step enrichment flow. Before hitting Apollo, it checked what fields were already populated. Before calling PDL as a fallback, it mapped which missing fields PDL could actually fill vs. which ones needed a different source entirely. It saved two unnecessary API calls and produced cleaner data on the first pass.

The gap isn't speed. It's error rate. Extended thinking produces fewer retries, fewer malformed payloads, fewer "why is this field null" debugging sessions.
remixes.cta: If you're building multi-step automations with Claude Code, run one build with extended thinking on and compare the output quality. The difference shows up in the details you'd otherwise spend an hour debugging.

remixes.label: mental-model-shift
remixes.hook: We keep treating extended thinking like a premium toggle. Turn it on for hard problems, off for simple ones. That framing is wrong.
remixes.body:
We keep treating extended thinking like a premium toggle. Turn it on for hard problems, off for simple ones. That framing is wrong.

Extended thinking isn't about difficulty. It's about decision density. A simple task with one decision point doesn't benefit much. A medium task with twelve sequential decisions benefits enormously.

Most GTM engineering work falls into that second category. You're not solving one hard problem. You're making a dozen small choices that compound. Which enrichment provider to hit first. How to handle a partial match. Whether to retry or skip. What format the CRM expects. Each choice is easy in isolation. The sequence is where things go sideways.

When I pair extended thinking with tool use in Claude Code, the model treats each decision as part of a chain rather than an isolated call. It remembers that step 4 depends on the output shape of step 2. It notices when a fallback provider returns data in a different schema and transforms it before passing it downstream.

This is what separates an agent from an automation. An automation follows a fixed path. An agent navigates a decision tree. Extended thinking is what makes that navigation reliable instead of random.

The real unlock isn't "thinking harder." It's thinking relationally across steps.
remixes.cta: Next time you're evaluating where to use extended thinking, don't ask "is this problem hard?" Ask "how many decisions does this workflow make?" That's a better predictor of impact.

posts.title: Prompt chains are not agents
posts.hook: Shipped a pipeline last week that retried a failed enrichment call, pivoted to a backup provider, and wrote the fallback logic itself. That's an agent. A linear prompt chain with try/catch is a script.
posts.body:
Shipped a pipeline last week that retried a failed enrichment call, pivoted to a backup provider, and wrote the fallback logic itself. That's an agent. A linear prompt chain with try/catch is a script.

The distinction matters because it changes what you build.

When I build GTM pipelines with Claude Code, the agent decides which enrichment provider to hit based on what data is missing. It reads the schema, checks what fields are null, picks the right API, handles rate limits, and writes the transformation. If Apollo doesn't have the mobile number, it tries a waterfall. If the waterfall fails, it flags the record and moves on instead of crashing the whole run.

That's not a prompt chain. That's an agent making decisions at runtime based on state.

Most of the "AI agent" tools I evaluate for clients are prompt chains with a nice UI. They work great on the demo data. They break the moment your input doesn't match the expected shape.

The tell: can your "agent" handle a situation it wasn't explicitly programmed for? If no, it's a script with an LLM call in the middle.

Nothing wrong with scripts. I write plenty of them. Just don't charge agent pricing for a for-loop.

remixes.label: taxonomy-teardown
remixes.hook: Your "AI agent" is a for-loop with an LLM inside it. And that's fine. Just stop calling it an agent.
remixes.body:
Your "AI agent" is a for-loop with an LLM inside it. And that's fine. Just stop calling it an agent.

Here's the taxonomy that actually matters:

A script runs the same steps every time. Input goes in, output comes out, the path is fixed. Most "AI automations" are scripts. They use an LLM to generate text at one step, but the flow is hardcoded.

A chain connects multiple LLM calls in sequence. Each step's output feeds the next step's input. Fancier than a script, but still linear. If step 3 fails, the chain fails. LangChain made these popular. They're useful. They're not agents.

An agent makes decisions at runtime about what to do next. It observes the result of an action and chooses its next action based on what it learned. It can retry with different parameters. It can abandon a path and try a different one. It can write new logic it didn't have when it started.

Last week my Claude Code agent hit an enrichment API that returned garbage data. It didn't retry the same call. It examined the response, determined the email format was invalid, switched to a different provider, validated the new result against the original input, and logged why it made the switch. Nobody told it to do any of that.

The distinction matters because it changes how you architect. Chains need error handling written in advance. Agents need good tools and clear constraints. Different design patterns entirely.
remixes.cta: Look at your current "agent" setup. If you can draw the execution path as a straight line before it runs, it's a chain, not an agent. That's not a criticism. It's a design decision that should be intentional.

remixes.label: show-the-receipts
remixes.hook: People keep asking me how agents are different from automation. So here's the actual log from a build that went sideways in a useful way.
remixes.body:
People keep asking me how agents are different from automation. So here's the actual log from a build that went sideways in a useful way.

I was building a lead enrichment pipeline. The spec was simple: take a list of domains, enrich with contact data, score, output a CSV.

Here's what an automation would do: call Provider A for each domain, format the results, write the CSV. If Provider A fails, throw an error or retry.

Here's what actually happened with Claude Code acting as the agent:

Step 1: Hit Provider A. Got results for 60% of domains. Noticed the remaining 40% had a pattern: they were all .io and .dev TLDs.

Step 2: Without being told, it hypothesized that Provider A had weak coverage for newer TLDs. Switched to Provider B for the remaining domains. Got 80% of those.

Step 3: For the final holdouts, it tried a different approach entirely. Pulled company LinkedIn pages, extracted employee names, and ran those through a people-search API.

Step 4: Wrote a summary of which provider worked best for which TLD pattern and suggested I route future requests accordingly.

None of steps 2 through 4 were in my instructions. The agent assessed, adapted, and improved the process as it ran. That's the difference. Not sophistication. Adaptability.
remixes.cta: The test for whether you have an agent or a script is simple: does it do something different the second time based on what happened the first time? If the answer is no, you have a script with good copy.

tones.advisor:
The distinction between prompt chains and genuine agents is one of the most consequential architectural decisions in AI-assisted GTM right now. Here's how I frame it for teams I work with.

A prompt chain is deterministic. You define the steps, the order, and the error handling in advance. The LLM generates text at certain nodes, but the flow is fixed. This is appropriate for well-understood, repeatable tasks where the failure modes are known.

An agent is adaptive. It observes outcomes and makes runtime decisions about what to do next. When an enrichment call returns partial data, it doesn't just retry or fail. It evaluates what's missing, determines which alternative source might fill the gap, and adjusts its approach.

I recommend teams ask three questions before choosing their architecture. First, are the failure modes known in advance? If yes, a chain with good error handling is simpler and more reliable. Second, does the task require multi-source reasoning? If the agent needs to compare outputs from different providers and choose the best result, you need agent-level decision making. Third, does the workflow need to improve over time? Agents can log their decisions and optimize routing. Chains run the same way every time.

Most teams I advise start with chains and graduate to agents only for workflows where adaptability creates measurable value. Don't over-engineer the simple stuff.
tones.provocateur:
Half the "agent" demos on LinkedIn are prompt chains wearing a trench coat. And the founders posting them know it.

A prompt chain calls an LLM, takes the output, passes it to the next step, and repeats. If something fails, it retries or throws an error. This is a script. A well-written script, maybe. But the execution path is identical every single time.

Last week I watched a Claude Code session handle something no chain could. An enrichment provider returned data that looked valid but had mismatched email domains. The agent caught the discrepancy, flagged the results as suspect, routed those contacts to a second provider for verification, and only included the ones that matched across both sources. Nobody programmed that workflow. The agent reasoned through it.

The industry has a branding problem. Calling everything an "agent" lets teams charge agent prices for script-level work. It lets founders claim autonomous AI capabilities for what is fundamentally a fancy webhook. And it confuses buyers who can't tell the difference.

Here's the test: can your "agent" handle a scenario you didn't anticipate when you built it? Not an edge case you forgot to code for. A genuinely novel situation. If it can't, you built a chain. Ship it as a chain. Price it as a chain.

posts.title: Claude Code changed my dev workflow permanently
posts.hook: I mass-deleted 3 SaaS subscriptions this month. Not because the products were bad. Because Claude Code builds the equivalent faster than I can log into the dashboard.
posts.body:
I mass-deleted 3 SaaS subscriptions this month. Not because the products were bad. Because Claude Code builds the equivalent faster than I can log into the dashboard.

One was a $200/mo enrichment orchestrator. Replaced it with a Python script that waterfalls through Apollo, PDL, and Dropcontact. Total API cost: maybe $40/mo. Runs on a cron. Claude Code wrote the whole thing in one session, including the SQLite tracking table and the dedup logic.

Another was a $150/mo reporting dashboard. Replaced it with a Next.js page that queries my own database. Same data, no middleman, no waiting for their export feature.

The third was a scheduling tool. Not worth discussing.

Tom Preston-Werner's point about Claude Code changing developer tooling hits different when you're a solo founder. For me it didn't just change how I code. It changed what I'm willing to pay for.

The calculus now: if a SaaS product is basically "reads data from A, transforms it, puts it in B," I build it. If it has genuine proprietary data or network effects, I buy it.

Most B2B SaaS is the first category.
posts.cta: What's the last tool you replaced with something you built yourself? Genuinely curious what categories are getting hit hardest.

remixes.label: cost-audit-breakdown
remixes.hook: I ran a cost audit on my SaaS stack last month. $740/mo in tools I could replace with scripts Claude Code writes in under an hour each. So I did.
remixes.body:
I ran a cost audit on my SaaS stack last month. $740/mo in tools I could replace with scripts Claude Code writes in under an hour each. So I did.

Here's the breakdown of what got cut and why.

Enrichment orchestrator, $200/mo. Replaced with a 180-line Python script that waterfalls through three providers. Runs on a cron job. Total API cost around $40/mo because I only call the expensive provider when the cheap one misses.

Scheduling tool, $50/mo. Replaced with a script that reads a JSON config, formats content per platform, and hits each API directly. Claude Code wrote the initial version and I've tweaked it maybe twice since.

Dashboard builder, $120/mo. Replaced with a Python script that pulls from my database, generates charts with matplotlib, and writes a markdown report. Takes 30 seconds to run. The commercial tool took longer to load.

The pattern isn't "AI replaces SaaS." It's more specific than that. The tools that got replaced shared three traits: they had simple data-in, data-out workflows. They charged primarily for a UI I didn't need. And their core logic was a sequence of API calls that a competent developer could write in an afternoon.

Not every tool fits this pattern. My CRM, my email sending infrastructure, my analytics platform. Those have network effects, integrations, and complexity that justify the cost. The ones I cut were essentially paid wrappers around APIs I already had access to.
remixes.cta: Run the audit on your own stack. For each tool, ask: is the value in the logic or in the UI? If you never open the dashboard and just need the output, you might be paying for a wrapper.

remixes.hook: Everyone celebrates replacing SaaS with code. Nobody talks about the three tools I tried to replace and immediately re-subscribed to.
remixes.body:
Everyone celebrates replacing SaaS with code. Nobody talks about the three tools I tried to replace and immediately re-subscribed to.

I've been on a tear this year replacing paid tools with Claude Code-built scripts. Cut $500+/mo in SaaS spend. Felt great. Then I tried to go further and learned where the line is.

Tool I tried to replace #1: a CRM with pipeline management. Claude Code can absolutely build a contacts database with deal stages. What it can't replicate is the mobile app my team checks between meetings, the integrations with email and calendar, and two years of historical data with associated notes. Resubscribed in 48 hours.

Tool #2: an email deliverability platform. I thought sending email was just SMTP. It is not. Domain warming, inbox placement testing, bounce handling, compliance. The platform handles fifty edge cases I didn't know existed. Back within a week.

Tool #3: a design tool. I can generate SVGs programmatically. But for anything requiring iteration, collaboration, or visual judgment, code is the wrong medium.

The tools worth replacing share a pattern: simple input/output, no UI dependency, core logic is API orchestration. The tools worth keeping have a different pattern: they encode domain expertise you don't have, they require real-time collaboration, or they manage complexity you'd rather not own.

Knowing the difference saves you from building something that costs more in maintenance time than the subscription ever did.
remixes.cta: Before you replace your next SaaS tool, ask: am I paying for the logic or for the expertise baked into it? If it's expertise, keep paying.

This pattern repeats constantly in the AI startup world. Teams provision for peak load, run at a fraction of it, and treat the bill as cost of doing business because "AI is expensive."

AI is expensive when you don't measure.

The fix in most cases isn't technical wizardry. It's basic ops:

✅ Spot instances for batch jobs (training, embedding generation, bulk inference)
✅ Auto-scaling that actually scales down, not just up
✅ Caching inference results for repeated queries
✅ Right-sizing your model... most production use cases don't need the biggest model available

I see the same pattern in GTM infrastructure. Teams pay for enterprise tiers of enrichment tools, use 10% of the features, and never audit the spend. The API calls they're making could run on a $50/mo plan if they batched properly.

Whether it's GPUs or GTM tools, the pattern is identical: provision for the ceiling, operate at the floor, never look at the dashboard.

The founders who survive the next 18 months will be the ones who actually read their usage metrics.

remixes.body:
I spent $9,200 on GPU compute last quarter before someone asked me what my actual utilization was. I didn't have an answer. So I looked.

31%.

I was paying for three reserved instances running 24/7 to handle a peak load that happened for about 4 hours a day. The rest of the time, those GPUs were sitting idle, burning cash at the same rate.

The fix took two days. I moved to spot instances for batch processing, set up auto-scaling for the inference endpoint, and kept one small reserved instance for low-latency requests that couldn't tolerate cold starts.

New monthly cost: $3,400. Same performance during peak. Slightly slower cold starts on batch jobs, which nobody noticed because batch jobs don't have users waiting on them.

The thing that bothers me isn't that I was wasting money. It's that I had accepted "AI is expensive" as a fact of life without ever measuring whether my specific implementation was expensive or just poorly configured.

I see this constantly now. Founders treating their GPU bill like rent. A fixed cost you can't control. But unlike rent, compute is elastic. You're choosing to pay for idle capacity every month you don't measure utilization.

The math isn't complicated. Pull your utilization metrics. If you're below 50%, you're almost certainly over-provisioned. The fix is usually auto-scaling, spot instances, or right-sizing. Not novel. Just neglected.
remixes.cta: Pull your compute utilization numbers today. Not the dashboard average. The per-instance, per-hour breakdown. You might find a 30-50% cost reduction hiding in plain sight.

remixes.label: checklist-framework
remixes.hook: Before your next board meeting, run this 5-point GPU spend audit. It takes 20 minutes and it might save you more than your last hire costs.
remixes.body:
Before your next board meeting, run this 5-point GPU spend audit. It takes 20 minutes and it might save you more than your last hire costs.

1. Pull per-instance utilization for the past 30 days. Not the aggregate average. Per-instance. If any instance is below 40% average utilization, it's a candidate for right-sizing or elimination.

2. Identify your peak hours. Most AI workloads have predictable traffic patterns. If your peak is 4 hours a day and you're running reserved instances 24/7, you're paying 6x what you need to outside those hours.

3. Separate batch from real-time. Batch processing (training runs, bulk inference, data processing) doesn't need reserved instances. Move these to spot or preemptible instances. They're 60-80% cheaper.

4. Check your instance types. Teams often provision the largest GPU available because it was easiest during setup. An A100 running inference on a model that fits on an A10 is like commuting in a semi truck.

5. Look at your storage. GPU instances often come with attached storage that persists even when the instance is stopped. Orphaned volumes and snapshots accumulate silently.

I ran this audit for a founder last week. He was spending $14k/mo. We found $8k in waste without changing a single line of application code. No performance degradation. Just right-sizing and scheduling.

The pattern is the same every time: teams provision for worst-case, never revisit, and normalize the bill.
remixes.cta: Run the five-point audit before your next finance review. Twenty minutes of measurement beats six months of "AI is expensive" assumptions.

posts.title: Outbound in 2026 still looks like 2022
posts.hook: Most outbound teams added AI to a broken process and called it innovation. They automated the wrong thing.
posts.body:
Most outbound teams added AI to a broken process and called it innovation. They automated the wrong thing.

The 2022 playbook: buy a list, write a sequence, blast it, pray for replies. The 2026 version: buy a list, have AI write a sequence, blast it faster, pray for replies.

Same motion. Higher volume. Same results.

The teams I work with that actually moved the needle changed the input, not the output. They stopped starting with a list and started starting with a signal.

Job posting mentions your competitor's integration? That's a signal. Company just raised a Series A and hired 3 SDRs in 30 days? Signal. Someone asked a question on Reddit about the exact problem you solve? That's the strongest signal of all.

The sequence still matters. The copy still matters. But if you're writing to someone who has no reason to care right now, the best copy in the world gets archived.

I built my outbound system around Reddit intent signals. Not because Reddit is magic. Because the person asking "how do I solve X" is further down the buying journey than someone on a purchased list who might have that problem.

Signal first. Sequence second. Volume last.
posts.cta: What signal sources are actually driving replies for your team right now? Not impressions. Replies.

remixes.label: signal-vs-volume
remixes.hook: A client replaced 50,000 cold emails per month with 2,000 signal-triggered messages. Their pipeline grew. The math shouldn't work. It does.
remixes.body:
A client replaced 50,000 cold emails per month with 2,000 signal-triggered messages. Their pipeline grew. The math shouldn't work. It does.

Here's what changed.

The old approach: buy a list of 10,000 contacts that match the ICP on paper. Write a five-email sequence. Send it. 0.3% reply rate. Maybe 15 conversations. Maybe 3 deals.

The new approach: monitor hiring signals, tech stack changes, funding events, and content engagement across the target account list. When a signal fires, send one highly relevant message within 48 hours. No sequence. No follow-up cadence. Just one message that references the specific thing that happened.

2,000 sends per month. 4.2% reply rate. 84 conversations. More deals from fewer sends with lower cost and zero spam complaints.

The insight isn't "personalization works." Everyone knows personalization works. The insight is that the input matters more than the output. Better targeting beats better copywriting every time. You can A/B test subject lines until you're blue in the face, but if you're emailing someone who has no reason to care right now, the best copy in the world won't fix that.

The teams winning at outbound in 2026 didn't upgrade their sequences. They upgraded their signal infrastructure. They know who to contact and when. The message almost writes itself after that.
remixes.cta: What signal sources are you actually monitoring right now? Not the ones in your deck. The ones that trigger a send within 48 hours.

remixes.label: autopsy-of-a-sequence
remixes.hook: I audited a 7-step outbound sequence last month. Step 1 had a 0.4% reply rate. Steps 2 through 7 combined had a 0.1% reply rate and generated 100% of the spam complaints.
remixes.body:
I audited a 7-step outbound sequence last month. Step 1 had a 0.4% reply rate. Steps 2 through 7 combined had a 0.1% reply rate and generated 100% of the spam complaints.

The team had spent weeks optimizing the copy for steps 3 through 7. A/B testing subject lines. Testing send times. Trying different CTAs. None of it moved the needle because the fundamental problem wasn't the message. It was the audience.

They were emailing people who had no reason to care. The list was built from firmographic filters: industry, company size, title. Technically correct ICP matches with zero timing signal. No recent hire. No tech stack change. No content engagement. No trigger event.

We scrapped steps 2 through 7 entirely. Redirected that effort into building signal detection. Job postings mentioning specific pain points. LinkedIn activity around relevant topics. G2 category research. Tech stack changes visible through BuiltWith.

New motion: one email, sent within 48 hours of a signal firing. The reply rate on that single email is higher than the entire old sequence combined.

 about outbound in 2026: AI made it trivially easy to send more email. That's exactly what most teams did. Volume went up. Deliverability went down. Inboxes got noisier. And the teams still winning are the ones who send less, not more.

Adding AI to outbound without changing the targeting model is like putting a turbocharger on a car driving in the wrong direction.
remixes.cta: Pull the per-step metrics on your active sequences. If steps 3 and beyond aren't pulling their weight, you don't have a copy problem. You have a targeting problem.

posts.title: Content that generates zero pipeline
posts.hook: Published 47 blog posts last year for a client. Total pipeline sourced from the blog: zero. Not low. Zero.
posts.body:
Published 47 blog posts last year for a client. Total pipeline sourced from the blog: zero. Not low. Zero.

The posts were well-written. SEO-optimized. Published on schedule. Shared on social. Checked every box on the content strategy template.

The problem: they were written for a search engine, not for a buyer.

Every post answered a generic question. "What is account-based marketing?" "How to improve sales productivity." The kind of content that ranks, gets traffic from people writing college papers, and generates exactly no revenue.

The fix wasn't more content. It was different content.

We killed the blog calendar and replaced it with three things:

1. Build logs from the actual product team showing how they solved customer problems
2. Comparison pages that addressed real buying objections (not "us vs. competitor" fluff, but actual workflow differences)
3. Reddit and community answers repurposed into long-form posts with the technical depth intact

Pipeline from content went from zero to 11 opps in 90 days.

The difference wasn't volume or quality. It was intent match. The old content attracted researchers. The new content attracted buyers.

If your content team can't trace a single deal back to a piece of content, the strategy isn't working. Doesn't matter how good the writing is.

remixes.hook: We audited a B2B company's content library. 112 published pieces. We could tie exactly one to a closed deal. One.
remixes.body:
We audited a B2B company's content library. 112 published pieces. We could tie exactly one to a closed deal. One.

The content team was producing two posts a week, hitting their KPIs on traffic and keyword rankings. Marketing dashboards looked healthy. But when we sat down with the sales team and asked which content actually came up in deal cycles, the room went quiet.

The one piece that worked? A detailed breakdown of how a customer migrated off a legacy vendor in 60 days. It wasn't SEO-optimized. It ranked for nothing. But the sales team sent it to every prospect stuck in evaluation, and it closed three deals in a quarter.

The other 111 posts were answering questions that buyers had already answered before they ever hit the website. Definitional content. Beginner guides. Stuff that attracts researchers, not buyers.

The fix wasn't producing more content. It was interviewing the sales team about the five questions that come up in every deal, then writing content that answers those specific objections with real customer proof.

Content strategy that starts with keyword research instead of pipeline data is working backwards. Start with the deals you lost and the questions that stalled them.
remixes.cta: Ask your sales team: which piece of content have you actually sent to a prospect this quarter?

remixes.label: content-graveyard-math
remixes.hook: Your company blog has 200 posts. Your sales team uses three of them. That's not a content strategy. That's a content graveyard.
remixes.body:
Your company blog has 200 posts. Your sales team uses three of them. That's not a content strategy. That's a content graveyard.

I started asking every head of content I met the same question: what percentage of your published library gets shared by sales in active deals? The average answer is somewhere around 2-3%. Most don't even know.

Here's what happened at one company when we flipped the model. Instead of the content calendar driving production, we recorded five sales calls, pulled out the twelve most common objections, and wrote a piece addressing each one. No keyword research. No SEO briefs. Just direct answers to the questions real buyers were actually asking.

Result: sales started forwarding those pieces unprompted. Two of them became the most-viewed pages on the site within 90 days, purely through direct shares and email signatures.

The irony is that buyer-first content often ends up ranking anyway, because it answers questions people actually search in buying mode, not learning mode.

Stop measuring content by volume published. Measure it by how often your sales team voluntarily sends it to a prospect without being asked.

The LinkedIn posts that generate pipeline have almost nothing in common with the posts that get likes. I learned this the hard way.

My highest-performing post by engagement was a meme about GTM tools. 200+ likes. Zero inbound. My highest-performing post by pipeline was a build log showing exactly how I replaced a $500/mo enrichment stack with Claude Code and three API keys. 60 likes. Four discovery calls.

The pattern I've seen across dozens of founders:

Posts that get likes: hot takes, relatable frustrations, industry drama, memes.

Posts that get pipeline: specific builds, real numbers, actual workflows someone can replicate or wants help implementing.

The first category builds audience. The second converts it. You need both, but most founders only post the first because the dopamine loop rewards engagement, not revenue.

The three things that consistently show up in pipeline-generating posts: a specific problem named clearly, the actual solution with enough detail to be credible, and a result that makes someone think "I need that for my team."

remixes.body:
I tracked 30 LinkedIn posts by two metrics: likes and inbound conversations. The correlation between them was almost perfectly inverse.

The posts that got 150+ likes were broad, relatable, easy to agree with. Hot takes on industry trends. Memes about the sales-marketing divide. Fun to engage with, zero commercial signal.

The posts that generated actual pipeline were boring by engagement standards. A teardown of how I built a specific workflow. A side-by-side comparison of two tools with actual numbers. A candid post-mortem on a project that went sideways.

These posts got 30-60 likes. But they attracted people who were actively trying to solve the same problem. The DMs started with "I'm dealing with exactly this" instead of "great post."

Here's the mechanism: broad content attracts a broad audience. Specific content attracts a specific audience. Pipeline comes from specificity because the people who respond are self-qualifying.

When someone DMs you about a build log showing how you cut enrichment costs by 80%, they're telling you they have the same problem and the budget to solve it.

I stopped optimizing for likes about six months ago. My engagement dropped. My inbound doubled. The math works out in one direction only.
remixes.cta: Next time you draft a post, ask: will this attract people who want to solve a problem, or people who want to agree with an opinion?

60 likes. Four discovery calls booked from the DMs within a week.

Build logs work because they do three things simultaneously. They demonstrate capability without claiming it. They qualify the reader by topic. And they give the prospect a reason to reach out that isn't "tell me more about your services."

Compare that to a thought leadership post about "the future of GTM." Everyone agrees, everyone likes it, nobody needs your help because you haven't shown them a problem they recognize.

The formula: pick something you built this week, document what you did and why, include the real numbers. Post it. The people who reach out are your buyers.

posts.title: Automated outbound without the soul
posts.hook: Fully automated outbound sounds great until you read the emails it sends. I built one. Then I rebuilt it.
posts.body:
Fully automated outbound sounds great until you read the emails it sends. I built one. Then I rebuilt it.

First version: Clay pulls the company data, Apollo grabs the contacts, Claude writes the first line, sequence fires automatically. Zero human touch. Felt like the future.

Then I read the emails from the recipient's perspective. They were technically personalized. They mentioned the right company name, the right role, even referenced a recent blog post. And they felt exactly like what they were... an AI that scraped my website and generated a sentence about it.

The personalization was correct but hollow. Like a stranger who memorized your LinkedIn before a networking event and recites it back to you.

Second version: same stack, different architecture. Clay and Apollo still do the research. But Claude's job changed. Instead of writing a personalized first line, it writes a research brief. I read the brief in 30 seconds, write one real sentence, and the sequence handles the rest.

30 seconds of human judgment per prospect. Reply rates went from 2.1% to 8.4%.

The lesson: automate the research, not the relationship. The moment you remove all human judgment from outbound, you're sending spam with better grammar.

Full automation is the goal for data ops. It's the wrong goal for the message.
posts.cta: Where do you draw the line between automation and human touch in your outbound?

inspired_by.author: Alexis Petrichor
inspired_by.summary: I built a fully automated outbound system using Clay, Apollo, and a Claude prompt that writes first lines personalized to each prospect's last LinkedIn post. Cost: $400/month in tooling. Output: 1,200 personalized emails per week with a 6.8% reply rate. Here's the exact workflow I use — no vendor deal, no affiliate link, just the build.

remixes.label: recipient-pov-test
remixes.hook: I BCC'd myself on 50 automated outbound emails my system sent. I would have deleted 47 of them. That's when I knew the system was broken.
remixes.body:
I BCC'd myself on 50 automated outbound emails my system sent. I would have deleted 47 of them. That's when I knew the system was broken.

The emails were technically correct. Right company info, right title, right industry reference. But reading them as a recipient, they felt hollow. Like a chatbot wearing a human mask. You could sense the automation even if you couldn't pinpoint it.

The problem wasn't the data or the personalization layer. The problem was that no one in the loop had read the output and asked "would I reply to this?"

So I rebuilt the system with one constraint: every email had to pass the inbox test. I opened my own inbox, put the outbound email next to the 30 other messages I received that day, and asked if it would survive the 2-second scan.

What changed: I killed the generic first lines. Stopped referencing company funding rounds nobody cares about. Added one specific observation about something the recipient actually built or shipped, pulled from their recent public work.

Reply rates went from 1.2% to 4.8%. Not because the automation got smarter, but because a human started reading the output before it went out.

The best outbound systems aren't fully automated. They're automated right up to the point where human judgment still matters, and that point is the final read.
remixes.cta: Open your sent folder. Read your last 10 outbound emails as if you received them. How many would you reply to?

remixes.label: automation-spectrum
remixes.hook: There's a spectrum between "send every email by hand" and "automate everything." Most teams pick one extreme and suffer. Here's what works in the middle.
remixes.body:
There's a spectrum between "send every email by hand" and "automate everything." Most teams pick one extreme and suffer. Here's what works in the middle.

I've built outbound systems at both ends. Manual-only tops out at 30 emails a day and burns out your SDRs. Full automation sends 500 a day but the quality is so low your domain reputation tanks within a month.

The system that actually worked automates research and drafting, but keeps a human in the review loop. Here's the split:

Automate: company research, contact finding, data enrichment, first-draft email generation, send scheduling, follow-up sequencing.

Keep human: reading the draft before it goes out, cutting the generic lines, adding one observation that proves you actually looked at their work, deciding whether this person is worth emailing at all.

That human review step takes about 15 seconds per email. At 200 emails a day, that's 50 minutes of human time. The rest is automated.

The result: 4x the volume of pure manual outbound, 3x the reply rate of pure automated outbound. The sweet spot exists, and it's not where most people think.

Full automation is a trap because it optimizes for volume at the expense of the one thing that matters: whether the recipient feels like a person wrote to them specifically.
remixes.cta: What's automated and what's human in your outbound stack right now? Where does the handoff happen?

posts.title: Solo founder $8k MRR with zero ads
posts.hook: The founders hitting $5-10k MRR with no ad spend all share one trait. It's not the product. It's the distribution they built before the product.
posts.body:
The founders hitting $5-10k MRR with no ad spend all share one trait. It's not the product. It's the distribution they built before the product.

I've watched this pattern repeat a dozen times in the last year. A solo founder ships a tool, hits paying customers in weeks, and everyone asks about the product.

Nobody asks about the 6 months of Reddit comments, niche community contributions, and build-in-public posts that came before launch.

The product gets the MRR. The distribution gets the product its first 50 users. And those first 50 users came from trust built in communities before the product existed.

This is why I built Clearbox around Reddit intent signals. The founders winning without paid ads aren't running some secret growth hack. They're present in the communities where their buyers already ask questions. They answer those questions genuinely. They build reputation. Then when they launch, those same people are the first customers.

Paid ads work. But they rent attention. Community presence builds an asset.

The tactical version: pick 3 subreddits or communities where your buyer hangs out. Answer questions for 90 days. Track which answers generate profile visits or DMs. Build the product that solves what they keep asking about.

Distribution before product. Every time.

A founder launched a dev tool last month. 200 paying users in 3 weeks. No Product Hunt, no ads, no launch event. Just 8 months of Reddit comments.

I asked him to walk me through his pre-launch activity. He'd been answering questions in three subreddits for 8 months. Not promoting anything. Just genuinely helping people solve the problem his product would eventually solve.

By launch day, his username was recognized in those communities. When he posted "I built a tool for this," the thread didn't get flagged as self-promotion. People vouched for him in the comments because they'd seen him helping for months.

First 200 customers came almost entirely from those communities. CAC was effectively zero. Not because the product was free to distribute, but because the distribution was built into the community presence he'd already established.

Contrast this with the standard playbook: build in silence for 6 months, launch on Product Hunt, buy ads, wonder why nobody cares. That founder is starting from zero trust with zero audience on launch day.

The distribution advantage isn't about building an audience. It's about building recognition in communities where your buyers already congregate. When you show up as a known contributor instead of a stranger with a product, the conversion math is completely different.

Distribution isn't a launch-day activity. It's a practice you start months before you have anything to sell.

Months before launch, they're active in 2-3 niche communities. Not posting about their product. Not building hype. Just answering questions and sharing what they've learned about the problem space.

This does two things. It builds name recognition with exactly the people who will eventually buy. And it gives the founder constant exposure to how real users describe the problem in their own words. That feedback loop shapes the product, the positioning, and the landing page copy.

By launch day, these founders aren't cold-starting. They have a warm network of people who already associate their name with the problem. The launch post reads like a natural next step, not an interruption.

Compare that to the founder who builds for 6 months, crafts a Product Hunt launch, and then realizes they're shouting into a void of people who've never heard of them.

The gap isn't in product quality. It's in the accumulated trust at launch.

Six months of community contribution before you build is worth more than $50k in ads after you launch. The math isn't even close.

posts.title: Ship speed is the new moat for AI products
posts.hook: 6 teams in the same YC batch building the same thing. The one that won shipped fastest and talked to customers most. Not the one with the best model.
posts.body:
6 teams in the same YC batch building the same thing. The one that won shipped fastest and talked to customers most. Not the one with the best model.

This is the reality of building AI products right now. The technology layer is increasingly commoditized. Claude, GPT, Gemini... they all handle most use cases well enough. The differentiator is speed to market and depth of customer understanding.

I see this in GTM engineering too. Three companies might build an "AI-powered enrichment" tool. The one that wins is the one that ships a working version to 10 customers this week, learns what breaks, and ships the fix by Friday.

Claude Code accelerated this cycle for me. I ship features in hours that used to take days. Not because the code is better. Because the iteration loop compressed.

Build Monday. Ship Tuesday. Get feedback Wednesday. Fix Thursday. Ship again Friday.
